Ethos is a noun with two closely related meanings — one used in everyday language, and one used specifically in writing, speaking, and the art of persuasion. Both meanings share the same core idea: character and trustworthiness. Understanding both will give you the full picture of this word.
The Everyday Meaning: The Spirit and Character of a Group

In everyday use, ethos refers to the underlying spirit, character, and core values that define a person, group, culture, profession, or historical era. It is not just what a group does — it is the deeper why behind what they do. It is the invisible force that shapes how people think, feel, behave, and make decisions. Think of ethos as the soul of a group.

A useful way to picture it: imagine walking into two different hospitals. One feels cold, bureaucratic, and impersonal. The other feels warm, attentive, and deeply human. Both may deliver the same medical care, but they feel completely different. That difference — that underlying attitude, that spirit, those unspoken priorities — is the ethos of each place.

The important thing to understand is that ethos is usually unspoken. It is not written in a rulebook. You sense it in how people behave, what they celebrate, what they refuse to do, and what they take pride in. Here is how the word looks in use:

"The ethos of the military is discipline, honor, and sacrifice." "Silicon Valley has an ethos of disruption — move fast, take risks, and challenge what already exists." "She was drawn to the ethos of the craftsman — patience, precision, and deep respect for one's work." "The 1960s counterculture had an ethos of peace, freedom, and resistance to authority."

It is also worth noting that while ethos most often describes groups, it can describe individuals too. A person can have a strong personal ethos — a consistent, deeply held set of values and principles that guides their life. "His entire career reflected a personal ethos of putting service before personal gain."
The Rhetorical Meaning: Credibility and Trust

The second meaning of ethos belongs to the world of rhetoric — the art of persuading people through writing or speech. Here, ethos refers specifically to the credibility, authority, and trustworthiness of the speaker or writer. It is the quality that makes an audience think: "I can trust this person. They know what they are talking about."

This meaning was defined by the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, who argued that there are three ways to persuade an audience: through logic (which he called logos), through emotion (which he called pathos), and through credibility (which he called ethos). Of the three, Aristotle considered ethos the most powerful, because if your audience does not believe in your character, nothing else you say will land.

When you read a book about heart disease written by a cardiologist with thirty years of clinical experience, you trust it partly because of the doctor's ethos — their expertise, their reputation, their integrity. When a politician says "I have spent twenty years working on this issue and I understand it from the inside," they are making a direct appeal to their ethos. When a writer opens an essay by sharing their own lived experience with a difficult subject, they are building ethos with the reader. In this sense, ethos is the answer to one specific question: Why should I believe you?

A speaker or writer builds ethos through their qualifications, their track record, their tone of fairness and honesty, and their demonstrated understanding of a subject. They can also lose their ethos — through a lie, a scandal, or a display of ignorance — and once ethos is lost, it is very hard to recover.
How Ethos Differs from Similar Words

Ethos is easy to confuse with nearby words, so it is worth drawing clear lines.

Ethics and ethos are related but not the same. Ethics refers to the rules and principles we use to judge whether something is right or wrong — it is more like a code or a framework. Ethos is the living spirit or character from which those ethical choices grow. Think of it this way: ethics is the law, ethos is the kind of person you are even when no one is watching.

Values are specific beliefs a group or person holds — honesty, loyalty, courage, and so on. Ethos is the total character that all those values create together when they are actually lived out. You could say values are the ingredients, and ethos is what the dish tastes like.

Culture refers to everything a group does — their customs, traditions, art, rituals, and language. Ethos is the driving spirit behind that culture, the reason the culture looks and feels the way it does.

Atmosphere or vibe is the mood you feel in a place. Ethos is deeper — it speaks to the moral and philosophical identity of a group, not just the feeling in the room at a given moment.

Ethos is a singular noun. Its technical plural is "ethoses," but you will almost never encounter it in the plural, because ethos usually describes one collective spirit at a time. The most common patterns are "the ethos of" — the ethos of a generation, the ethos of a workplace — and "an ethos of" — an ethos of excellence, an ethos of inclusion. The verbs most commonly paired with ethos are: embody, reflect, shape, define, capture, uphold, challenge, and lose.
More Examples to Make It Stick

"The company's ethos is built on radical honesty — nothing is hidden from employees, not even bad news." "As a journalist, her personal ethos demanded that she never reveal a confidential source, no matter the pressure." "His speech was powerful not just because of the evidence he presented, but because of the strong personal ethos he projected — he had lived through exactly what he was describing." "The Renaissance had an ethos of human possibility: the belief that a single individual could master art, science, and philosophy all at once." "When the CEO was caught lying to investors, the company didn't just face a legal problem — it lost the ethos it had spent decades building."

In short: when ethos describes a group or person, it means the deep, defining character and spirit that drives them. When ethos describes a speaker or writer, it means the credibility and trustworthiness that makes people believe them. Both uses come back to the same root idea — the genuine, lived character of a person or group, which cannot be faked for long.
